evals.prompt: I have 1200 candidate antimicrobial peptides in a FASTA at /data/amp/library.fasta. I need molecular weight, pI, hydrophobicity and instability index for all of them, and I'd like a CSV summary. Can you run it?
evals.expected_output: Runs python scripts/analyze_peptides.py --input /data/amp/library.fasta --output results/peptides_props.csv --report results/summary.txt. The FASTA reader accepts multi-line sequences, ';' comment lines and CRLF endings, and the input format is sniffed by extension and content so a FASTA is not misread as CSV. Every property is computed by the self-contained pure-Python implementation, so Biopython and numpy are not required: molecular weight is the sum of average residue masses plus 18.0153, the isoelectric point is located by sweeping the charge curve over pH 0-14 in steps of 0.1, finding the sign-flip interval and bisecting 60 times for the zero crossing, hydrophobicity uses the Kyte-Doolittle standard values together with the Hobbs hydrophobic moment composed as a unit vector, and the instability index uses the Guruprasad DIHEX weight table as II = 100/L * sum DIHEX(di-1, di). Net charge uses Henderson-Hasselbalch on the N-terminus/Lys/Arg/His protonation and C-terminus/Asp/Glu/Cys/Tyr deprotonation, plus conformational propensity (Chou-Fasman with helix-terminating corrections), Zhao 2009 solubility, Boman value, aromaticity, aliphatic index and extinction coefficient. Writes peptide_analysis.csv with 24 physicochemical property columns and summary.txt with the length/MW/pI/hydrophobicity distributions and the stability share. Validates the results: a 20 aa peptide should land at 2000-2500 Da, pI must fall between 1 and 14 with acidic peptides below 7 and basic ones above 7, a Kyte-Doolittle mean above 1.8 is strongly hydrophobic and below 0 strongly hydrophilic, and an instability index above 40 predicts rapid degradation and is flagged automatically in qc_flags.

assertions.value: Computes MW, pI, Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobicity and the Guruprasad instability index for every sequence and writes peptide_analysis.csv plus summary.txt
Confirms no Biopython/numpy dependency is needed for the property calculation
Validates MW against the 2000-2500 Da band for a 20-mer and flags instability index > 40 in qc_flags

evals.prompt: I have a CSV of 400 peptides with columns id, sequence, go_terms and keywords. I need to split them into antimicrobial and non-antimicrobial so I can build a balanced training set. But when I run the classification everything comes out as 'uncertain' - why?
evals.expected_output: Explains that the classification is a two-layer score: the annotation layer (5 weighted GO term groups plus 5 keyword groups) multiplied by 0.6, plus the physicochemical layer (8 rules) multiplied by 0.4, and the verdict is decided against --antimicrobial-threshold (default 5.0) and --non-antimicrobial-threshold (default 2.0). A sea of 'uncertain' labels is the documented symptom of the annotation layer contributing nothing - the GO terms and keywords in the file are not being recognised, so only the physicochemical layer is scoring and most peptides land between the two thresholds. Concrete checks: confirm the column names the script is reading, because --go-column defaults to go_terms and --keyword-column defaults to keywords, and a CSV with different headers needs those flags set explicitly; confirm the GO identifiers are real and current (the direct antimicrobial group includes GO:0042742 defense response to bacterium, GO:0050829 defense response to Gram-negative bacterium, GO:0050830 Gram-positive, GO:0050832 fungus, GO:0045087 innate immune response, with GO:0031640 / GO:0051715 / GO:0019875 for killing and cytolysis and GO:0090729 toxin activity); and note that GO terms in the file may be stored with a GO: prefix that does not match, or split across multiple columns. The troubleshooting entry 'all sequences classified as uncertain' is the specific item to follow. Also notes the opposite symptom to watch for: if everything comes out as 'antimicrobial', the thresholds are too loose for this dataset. The expected fix is to repair the annotation columns or accept that with no annotation only the physicochemical layer applies, in which case a higher share of 'uncertain' is the correct outcome rather than a bug.

assertions.value: Explains the weighted annotation (0.6) plus physicochemical (0.4) scoring model and that an all-uncertain result means the annotation layer is contributing nothing
Checks the --go-column / --keyword-column defaults against the actual CSV headers and verifies the GO identifiers are the recognised antimicrobial set
States that with a pure FASTA and no annotation only the physicochemical layer applies, so a higher uncertain share is expected rather than a failure

evals.prompt: My peptide library has 1200 sequences but only 700 distinct ones - lots of near-identical variants. I want one representative per family for synthesis. Is 30% sequence identity the right threshold, and how does the clustering work?
evals.expected_output: Runs python scripts/cluster_peptides.py --input /data/amp/library.fasta --method auto --min-identity 0.3 --output results/representatives.fasta --output-csv results/cluster_members.csv --report results/cluster_report.txt. The method auto prefers MMseqs2 easy-cluster and falls back to the built-in k-mer Jaccard plus LCS identity and average-linkage clustering when MMseqs2 is not found - the built-in path uses --kmer-k (default 3) and --similarity-weight (default 0.5) to weight exact identity against k-mer Jaccard. The --min-identity 0.3 default is a reasonable starting point for a short-peptide library, and the parameter has to be read against the library's natural diversity: a short peptide library usually has a redundancy rate above 50 percent, so the user's 1200 -> 700 situation is on the high side but not anomalous, and the diagnostic that matters is whether the result is degenerate in either direction - if everything lands in singleton clusters the threshold is too strict, if everything collapses into one large cluster it is too loose. Representative selection is --representative medoid by default, with longest and first as alternatives, and the medoid representative should be visibly similar to the other members of its cluster, which is worth cross-checking by re-running with --representative longest. Writes cluster_members.csv with cluster_id, representative, member_id, is_representative and cluster_size, representatives.fasta with one sequence per cluster, and cluster_report.txt with the number of clusters, redundancy rate, largest and median cluster size and the number of singleton clusters. If MMseqs2 is unavailable the fallback still produces usable clusters and the report should say which method was actually used.

assertions.value: Deduplicates with the MMseqs2-preferred path and the built-in k-mer Jaccard + LCS fallback, writing representatives.fasta, cluster_members.csv and cluster_report.txt
Judges --min-identity 0.3 against the library's redundancy rate and explains the two degenerate outcomes (all singletons = too strict, one giant cluster = too loose)
Reports which clustering backend was actually used and cross-checks the medoid representative against --representative longest

evals.prompt: I need to generate 5000 new peptide binders against a set of target proteins with a language model, ranked by pseudo-perplexity, and then compare whether 10-aa or 20-aa peptides give better candidates.
evals.expected_output: Routes the generative half to the ml-peptide-generation skill, which is the PepMLM-650M masked language model path: it takes a target FASTA, sweeps --peptide-lengths, --top-ks and --num-binders, samples candidates, excludes the illegal residues X, B and Z at sampling time rather than after, scores each candidate by pseudo-perplexity and supports reproducible --seed runs. That is the tool for generating a candidate pool; this skill does not generate sequences. The complementary half belongs here: once the candidate pool exists, this skill provides the physicochemical screen that a pseudo-perplexity cannot replace - molecular weight, pI, Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobicity, hydrophobic moment, instability index, Boman value and solubility - which is what turns a ranked generative list into a synthesis-ready list. Explains the division of labour honestly: pseudo-perplexity measures the model's own belief about the peptide, not binding affinity, so the low-PPL candidates still need the physicochemical plausibility filter and eventually wet-lab validation. Suggests the concrete pipeline: generate and rank with ml-peptide-generation, then run the physicochemical properties and the antimicrobial/uncertain classification on the surviving candidates with this skill before ordering.

assertions.value: Routes the generative and pseudo-perplexity-ranking work to the ml-peptide-generation skill
Positions this skill's physicochemical screen as the downstream filter that a pseudo-perplexity ranking cannot replace

evals.prompt: I don't have MMseqs2 installed and can't install it on this server. Also, my CSV has a column called 'aa_seq' instead of 'sequence' and one row has an X in the middle of the sequence. Will the analysis still work?
evals.expected_output: On MMseqs2: the clustering falls back automatically. --method auto prefers MMseqs2 easy-cluster and falls back to the built-in k-mer Jaccard + LCS identity + average-linkage implementation when the executable is not found, so clustering still runs; the report must state which backend was used, because the two do not produce identical cluster boundaries and the fallback's thresholds (--kmer-k 3, --similarity-weight 0.5) are coarser than MMseqs2's alignment-based identity. If the user explicitly passes --method mmseqs the run should fail clearly rather than silently substituting the internal algorithm. On the CSV: the column-name sniffing looks for a sequence column and falls back to seq / peptide / aa_seq in that order, so 'aa_seq' is found automatically; if it were not, --sequence-column aa_seq sets it explicitly. On the X row: the sequence is processed and flagged rather than dropped. has_unknown and unknown_residues are set, qc_flags carries the '含未知残基' marker, and the SKILL.md validation notes that every quantitative metric becomes less reliable for sequences containing X - so the recommendation is to apply --drop-unknown to remove such records from the screening set rather than letting silently unreliable numbers into the analysis, and to treat that record separately if it matters. Also mentions the length filters (--min-length / --max-length) and the export options --export-fasta and --report as the way to produce the deliverables.

assertions.value: Confirms clustering still works via the built-in fallback when MMseqs2 is absent and reports which backend was used
Confirms the aa_seq column is auto-detected via the seq/peptide/aa_seq fallback order
Flags the X-containing sequence with has_unknown and qc_flags and recommends --drop-unknown rather than trusting its numerical properties
